summary:
No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding is documented for Córdoba. A trans visitor here stands under Colombia's national framework and is assessed against the national position rather than against any local deviation.

Two national patterns bear on what a visitor might face. The first is that lethal anti-trans violence can occur in daylight, be filmed, and leave the perpetrator unarrested: on 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon, police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after the president ordered an urgent investigation. Nationally, 13 trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, alongside earlier killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper.

The second pattern is territorial violence and displacement of trans people by armed actors. In Caquetá department, armed groups ran a 'social cleansing' campaign in which flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets; a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend was killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work.
tangentialFactors:
The national figures cited here are raw counts for the country as a whole and are not adjusted for population; they indicate the direction of risk rather than a per-capita rate, and no per-capita denominator is provided in the sources.

The Caquetá account concerns a different department from Córdoba and is included as an illustration of the pattern of armed-actor targeting of trans people, not as evidence of conditions in Córdoba itself.
localsOnly: No resident-facing legal, administrative or institutional finding specific to Córdoba is documented in the sources. Trans residents of the department stand under Colombia's national framework on legal gender recognition, identification markers, facilities access and partner recognition, which the parent record carries.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the armed-group 'social cleansing' flyer campaigns documented in Guajira and Caquetá have extended into Córdoba is unresolved; the sources do not address the department either way.

Enforcement of national protections, and any local police or official practice in Córdoba, are not sourced here and remain unverified.
